items.label: text
items.text: This is a displacement (or competition) reaction. Hydrogen is more reactive than copper and displaces it from copper oxide. Displacement reactions are discussed in Chapter 14.

items.label: text
items.text: The equation for the reaction that occurs in this experiment is:

items.label: text
items.text: CuO + H2 Cu + H2O copper(Ill) + hydrogen → copper + water oxide

items.label: text
items.text: As well as a displacement reaction, this type of reaction can also be called a redox reaction. Redox reactions are discussed in Chapter 14.

items.label: text
items.text: A set of results for this practical could be:

items.label: table
items.text:
| mass of empty dish/g                           |   23.78 |
|------------------------------------------------|---------|
| mass of dish + copper oxide/g                  |   26.96 |
| mass of dish + contents at end of experiment/g |   26.32 |

items.label: text
items.text: The reason that the mass decreases is because the hydrogen combines with the oxygen from the copper oxide to form water. The oxygen is removed from the copper oxide and we are left with only copper in the dish at the end of the experiment. Because oxygen is removed from the copper oxide we say that the copper oxide has been reduced. Reduction is explained in Chapter 14.

items.label: text
items.text: We can work out the mass of copper remaining at the end by subtracting the mass of the dish from the mass of the dish + copper at the end.

items.label: text
items.text: The mass has decreased because the oxygen has been removed from the copper oxide and we can calculate the mass of oxygen by subtracting the mass of copper at the end from the mass of copper oxide:

items.label: text
items.text: We now know that 2.54 g of copper combines with 0.64 g of oxygen in copper oxide and can deduce the empirical formula:

items.text:

|------------------------------------------------------------------------------|--------------|-------------|
| masses/g                                                                     | 2.54         | 0.64        |
| find the number of moles of atoms by dividing the mass by the mass of 1 mole | 2.54/63.5    | 0.64/16     |
| number of moles of atoms                                                     | 0.0400       | 0.040       |
| divide by the smaller number to find the ratio                               | 0.0400/0.040 | 0.040/0.040 |
| ratio of moles                                                               | 1            | 1           |
| empirical formula                                                            | CuO          | CuO         |
